11.event_title: Parakramabahu I builds the Parakrama Samudra reservoir
11.event: King Parakramabahu I, under whom the Polonnaruwa kingdom reached its greatest prosperity, built the great reservoir known as the Parakrama Samudra, the Sea of Parakrama. Britannica describes it as the crowning glory of his reign, with a storage area of more than 5,000 acres serving the irrigation of about 18,000 acres. The reservoir, formed by joining older tanks with new ones built in his reign, still holds water today.
11.explanation: A whole kingdom's prosperity was built on capturing and storing the monsoon rain, and the reservoir has continued to sustain farming for more than eight centuries.
11.tie_back: The kural calls rain the nectar by which the world keeps living, and Parakramabahu's vast tank shows a state treating every season's rainfall as the treasure on which its life depended.
11._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of rain as the life-sustaining wealth of a society, though it shows human engineering more than rain itself.

12.event_title: The Nabataeans harvest rainwater at Petra
12.date: Nabataean period, flourishing in Hellenistic and Roman times
12.event: The Nabataeans made Petra, in an arid region between the Red Sea and the Dead Sea, the rock-cut capital of their kingdom and a major caravan centre. They built channels, tunnels, diversion dams and a vast network of cisterns and reservoirs that controlled and conserved the seasonal rains. This water system allowed a large population to live in an essentially arid area.
12.explanation: Petra shows a desert city whose food, drink and very existence depended on catching rain that fell only in one season.
12.tie_back: The kural says rain both produces the food people eat and is itself their drink, and Petra's cisterns and channels kept the stored rain serving the city in both ways.
12._accuracy_note: Fits the dual role of rain as food-maker and drink, though the sources stress the engineering rather than the kural's double claim.

13.place: Shandong, Shanxi, Henan, Zhili and Shaanxi provinces, China
13.event: A long drought struck large parts of northern China from 1876, spreading from Shandong westward through Shanxi, Henan and beyond. Harvests failed and famine reached its peak in Shanxi and Henan in 1878; official accounts stated that Shanxi lost about half of its population. Estimates of the total death toll range from about nine to thirteen million people.
13.explanation: It was one of the deadliest famines of the 19th century, and it was triggered by rains that simply did not come.
13.tie_back: The kural warns that if the sky breaks faith and withholds rain, hunger will take up residence in the wide world, and the North China Famine is that warning carried out on a vast scale.
13._accuracy_note: Very close to a dramatisation of the kural: the failure of rain directly produced mass hunger.

14.event_title: The Dust Bowl drives farmers off the Great Plains
14.event: Severe drought struck the southern Great Plains in the 1930s, and crops began failing from 1931. Without deep-rooted prairie grasses to hold the over-ploughed soil, it blew away in great dust storms. With no way to make a living, many farm families abandoned their land, and hundreds of thousands of people left the region.
14.explanation: The Dust Bowl showed how quickly a farming society collapses when the rain on which its ploughing depends fails.
14.tie_back: The kural says that when rain, the great source of a land's yield, fails, even farmers stop driving the plough, and the Dust Bowl saw farm families abandon their fields entirely.
14._accuracy_note: A strong match, with the honest caveat that poor soil practices as well as drought caused the disaster.

15.event_title: Egypt completes the Aswan High Dam
15.event: After about eleven years of construction, the Aswan High Dam across the Nile was completed in 1970. Its main purpose was to store enough water in its reservoir, Lake Nasser, to protect Egypt from years when the Nile flood was too high or too low. The dam ended the old cycle of damaging floods and droughts along the Egyptian Nile.
15.explanation: Egypt built one of the world's largest dams because the same seasonal waters that made its farmland fertile could also ruin it, by flooding or by failing.
15.tie_back: The kural says rain both ruins people and raises them up again, and the Aswan High Dam was built precisely to manage the waters that had long done both to Egypt.
15._accuracy_note: Captures rain's double power to ruin and to restore, though the Nile flood comes from distant rainfall rather than local rain.

16.place: West African Sahel (including Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso and Chad)
16.event: From 1968 the rains in the West African Sahel deteriorated, and only in the 1974 rainy season did near-normal conditions return. The long drought led to the near-total failure of crops and the loss of an estimated 50 to 70 percent of cattle, with the pastoral grazing zones of the northern Sahel hit hardest. Large numbers of people died or were displaced by the resulting food shortages.
16.explanation: When the rains failed, the grasslands that supported herds across the Sahel withered, and a whole pastoral way of life collapsed with them.
16.tie_back: The kural says that without drops from the sky not even the tip of a blade of grass will be seen, and the Sahel's dying pastures showed the humblest green life vanishing first.
16._accuracy_note: A strong match: loss of pasture after rain failure is close to the kural's own image.

17.event_title: Pierre Perrault measures rain and river flow in the Seine basin
17.event: In his book De l'origine des fontaines, published in 1674, Pierre Perrault made quantitative estimates of rainfall and of river discharge in part of the Seine basin. He showed that rainfall was more than enough to sustain the flow of rivers and springs, refuting older theories that rivers were fed by seawater returning underground. His work, followed by that of Edme Mariotte and Edmond Halley, marked the start of quantitative study of the water cycle.
17.explanation: Perrault helped establish that the world's waters move in a closed cycle in which rain is the essential link.
17.tie_back: The kural describes the cloud drawing water from the sea and having to give it back, and Perrault's measurements began the scientific proof that rain is the link that keeps that cycle full.
17._accuracy_note: Matches the kural's water-cycle insight, but Perrault studied rivers rather than the sea's own fullness.

18.event_title: Megadroughts contribute to the decline of Angkor
18.event: Tree-ring records show that Angkor, the capital of the Khmer Empire and its great temple complex, suffered decades-long droughts in the mid-14th and early 15th centuries, separated by periods of intense monsoon flooding. Researchers conclude that these climate extremes strained the city's water system and, together with other factors, contributed to Angkor's decline as a capital.
18.explanation: Even one of the greatest temple cities ever built depended on reliable monsoon rain, and its long decline followed the failure of that rain.
18.tie_back: The kural warns that if the sky dries up, the festivals and daily worship of a land cannot go on, and Angkor's temple capital weakened when its monsoon failed.
18._accuracy_note: Drought is one documented contributor among several, and the sources do not record worship ending, so the fit is partial.

19.event_title: The Ancestral Pueblo people leave Mesa Verde during the Great Drought
19.event: The last tree-ring date for new construction in the Mesa Verde region is 1281. A drought lasted from 1276 through 1299, probably causing food shortages for a large population, and by about 1300 the Ancestral Pueblo people had left Mesa Verde and the Four Corners region, moving south into present-day New Mexico and Arizona. The National Park Service notes that drought combined with other stresses, such as depleted land and resources.
19.explanation: A long-settled society with rich communal and ceremonial life could not continue in its homeland once the rain failed for a generation.
19.tie_back: The kural says that without rain neither giving to others nor disciplined religious life can remain in the world, and Mesa Verde's whole community life left with the rains.
19._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the sources document migration after drought, not the specific collapse of charity and austerity the kural names.

20.date: Medieval origins; still meets weekly (UNESCO recognition 2009)
20.event: The Water Tribunal of the Plain of Valencia, whose roots go back to the al-Andalus period, meets every Thursday at noon at the Apostles' Door of Valencia Cathedral to settle disputes among farmers over irrigation water. Its members are elected representatives of the irrigation districts, its proceedings are oral, and its rulings are not appealed. In 2009 UNESCO inscribed it, with the Council of Wise Men of Murcia, on its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
20.explanation: For about a thousand years a community has kept its water flowing fairly by keeping its people's conduct in order, showing how closely right conduct and water are bound together.
20.tie_back: The kural plays on a word that means both flowing water and right conduct, and the Valencia tribunal is a living institution in which the flow of water and the order of conduct are kept together.
20._accuracy_note: A neat illustration of water and conduct bound together, though it concerns irrigation water rather than rain itself.
